    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Supreme Court on Monday denied review in several notable cases, including a clash between the Trump administration and University of California scholars over cuts to research funding; a California ophthalmologist’s challenge to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses; and a dispute over Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.” It also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks. These denials and requests were part of a list of orders from the justices’ private conference on Friday that was released on Monday morning.

    The court previously announced, just after Friday’s conference concluded, that the justices had added two cases to this term’s oral argument docket: Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, on whether the Trump administration can suspend access to asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border; and Robinhood Markets, Inc. v. Sodha, on whether a financial-services manufacturer violated federal securities laws when it failed to disclose some interim financial data as part of its initial public offering.

    The research funding case, Trump v. Thakur, stemmed from a series of executive orders issued by President Donald Trump soon after he began his second term, which addressed, among other things, efforts to reduce government spending and the withdrawal of government support from “diversity, equity, and inclusion” (DEI) initiatives. Federal agencies responded to the orders by cutting grant funding for projects they linked to disfavored topics, including DEI, which, in turn, led to lawsuits from states, universities, and individual scholars challenging the funding cuts.

    Industry observers note that thakur involved a group of faculty members and researchers at the University of California who lost research grants because of the executive orders. They challenged the grant terminations on behalf of a class of other UC scholars like them, contending that the administration had violated free speech and due process protections, as well as the federal law governing administrative agencies.

    Sources indicate that in June 2025, a federal district court in California issued a preliminary injunction requiring the Trump administration to reinstate grants for members of two overlapping classes: 1) UC researchers who were notified of a grant cut “by means of a form termination notice that does not provide a grant-specific explanation for the termination”; and 2) UC researchers who lost grant funding due to the DEI-related executive orders. The court held that cuts affecting the first group were likely to be found to be “arbitrary and capricious” – that is, lacking good cause and without providing a sound reason – in violation of the federal law governing administrative agencies and that cuts affecting the second group were likely to be found to violate the First Amendment.

    The Trump administration appealed to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, which initially denied the government’s request to put the district court’s ruling on hold. However, that same day, the Supreme Court sided with the administration in National Institutes of Health v. American Public Health Association, an interim docket case that also addressed research funding. A divided Supreme Court paused a ruling from a federal court in Massachusetts that would have required NIH to pay grants it had moved to terminate, holding that the lower court did not have the power to rule on claims “‘based on’ the research-related grants or to order relief designed to enforce any ‘obligation to pay money’ pursuant to those grants.” In light of the Supreme Court’s decision, the government asked the 9th Circuit to reconsider. In an amended order issued in December 2025, the 9th Circuit granted part of the government’s request.

    Sources indicate that in a May 2026 ruling, the 9th Circuit pointed to the Supreme Court decision to explain why it was reversing the lower court’s ruling as to the class of researchers who had received form letters from the government about their grants. As in the NIH case, the district court likely lacked the authority to hear the claim involving that class and to require grant reinstatement, the 9th Circuit concluded.

    However, the 9th Circuit affirmed the other part of the district court’s ruling, agreeing that members of the second class of researchers were likely to succeed on their claim that ending research grants over concerns about DEI violated the First Amendment. Although “the government has discretion to define subsidy programs in a way that reflects its preference to fund (or not fund) particular activities,” the 9th Circuit concluded, the Supreme Court has held that, once a subsidy program is established, the government “may not discriminate between speakers within that program to suppress viewpoints with which it disagrees.”.

    In August, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to review this second part of the 9th Circuit’s ruling, contending that it “conflicts with” Supreme Court precedent and “also interferes with executive-branch priorities in spending taxpayer funds, establishing a dangerous precedent that will hamstring every future administration when seeking to subsidize private projects that promote viewpoints aligned with government policy.” The First Amendment “does not require taxpayers to continue funding projects that the government concludes no longer serve the public interest,” asserted U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer.

    Recent findings suggest that in their brief opposing review, the researchers contended that the case was a poor candidate for review because the 9th Circuit’s decision does not conflict with any other federal appeals court or Supreme Court ruling. They further argued that the Trump administration failed to account for the fact that it is attempting to cut off already approved funds. “[T]he government can point to no case where this Court, or any court, has held that the President and federal agencies may terminate grants awarded through a merit-driven competitive process based on the perceived viewpoint of the research,” the researchers wrote.

    On Monday, the Supreme Court denied the Trump administration’s petition without comment or noted dissent.

    DEI and continuing education for doctors.

    Industry observers note that khatibi v. Yip also involved the First Amendment and DEI. It was brought to the Supreme Court by a California ophthalmologist, Dr. Azadeh Khatibi, who seeks to challenge the requirement, imposed by that state’s Medical Board, that continuing medical education courses include information about “the understanding of implicit bias” – that is, subconscious assumptions about people from different backgrounds.

    Recent findings suggest that khatibi, who frequently teaches continuing education classes, and a group of doctors went to federal court, where they argued that the requirement violates the First Amendment. U.S. District Judge Monica Ramirez Almadani dismissed the case, ruling that the courses are government speech and therefore not subject to the First Amendment’s free speech clause.

    After the 9th Circuit affirmed Ramirez Almadani’s decision, the doctors came to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to take up their case. They argued that Khatibi and other instructors like her “create and deliver their own original CME content without State drafting, editing, assignment of topics, or meaningful oversight.” If the lower court’s ruling is allowed to stand, they said, it “would license states to conscript private professionals—doctors, lawyers, teachers, engineers, and others—into advancing contested government ideologies whenever their instruction occurs in a licensure-related setting.”.

    The Medical Board urged the justices to deny review. It emphasized that the problem at the heart of the dispute is “narrow,” and that the 9th Circuit had “merely held that” the challengers “must abide by the State’s restrictions if they wish the courses that they teach be eligible for state-approved CME credit.”.

    It has been revealed that on Monday, the Supreme Court denied the petition over objections from three justices. Justice Neil Gorsuch indicated, without explanation, that he would grant the petition for review. Justice Clarence Thomas, joined by Justice Samuel Alito, wrote an opinion dissenting from the denial of review, in which he asserted that the 9th Circuit’s decision in Khatibi’s case “fundamentally misunderstands” Supreme Court “precedents and the Constitution.” According to Thomas, “First Amendment protections do not give way simply because a State heavily regulates speech.”.

    The Second Amendment and “sensitive places”.

    Industry observers note that thomas also wrote a statement regarding the Supreme Court’s decision to deny review in Novotny v. Moore, a Second Amendment challenge to Maryland laws banning firearms in a wide variety of public places, such as government buildings, school grounds, public transportation, state parks, stadiums, and places that sell alcohol.

    Industry observers note that in rejecting the challenge to the restrictions, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 4th Circuit relied on the idea, set out in the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen, that the right to carry a gun in public does not apply in “sensitive places.” In their petition for review, the challengers contended that “[t]he constitutionality of these so-called ‘sensitive place’ bans is among the most critical questions facing the judiciary in the wake of this Court’s decision in” Bruen. They argued that the court’s precedent makes clear that although governments may impose some gun restrictions in “sensitive places,” that exception is a “narrow” one.

    Recent findings suggest that maryland countered that there is no need for the Supreme Court to weigh in on this question now because there are “vast areas of shared consensus” among the lower courts with regard to restrictions on where guns may be carried and the rationale for such limits. The state pointed to what it characterized as a “[r]ich” historical tradition of laws that “restricted the carrying of firearms in specific locations.” The laws at matter in this case, the state remarked, “are consistent with” those laws “and the underlying principles of firearm regulation that they embody.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in his statement, Thomas described himself as “skeptical” of the 4th Circuit’s conclusion that each of the challenged restrictions “‘is consistent with this Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation’ in ‘sensitive places.’” But he explained that he agreed with the justices’ decision to deny the petition for review, because “the breadth” of the challenge to Maryland’s many policies “would complicate” the Supreme Court’s consideration of the case. “In an appropriate and more narrowly focused case, however,” Thomas continued, “we should consider the scope of States’ authority to ban firearms in ‘sensitive places.’”.

    The Supreme Court denied review in dozens of other cases on Monday, including disputes over how the federal judiciary handles sexual harassment and employment discrimination claims and the Colorado General Assembly’s rules for referring to transgender or nonbinary individuals during committee hearings.

    Strickland v. Moritz involved a former federal public defender in North Carolina who contends that she was sexually harassed by her supervisor. At problem in the case was the adequacy of the internal system that the federal judiciary requires its employees to use for sexual harassment and employment discrimination claims.

    Gays Against Groomers v. Garcia was a challenge by the nonprofit Gays Against Groomers, which describes itself as a group of “gays, lesbians, and others in the community” who are opposed to the transgender “agenda,” to the Colorado General Assembly’s ban on referring to transgender or nonbinary people by the wrong gender or by the name they used before their transition in legislative hearings. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit turned away the lawsuit, holding that “the establishment and enforcement of rules of decorum for legislative proceedings fall within the sphere of legitimate legislative activity,” and are therefore protected by legislative immunity.

    According to recent reports, and in Custodia Bank v. Federal Reserve Board of Governors, the justices turned down an appeal brought by a Wyoming bank after the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas turned down its application for an account with that bank. The Fed’s decision rested on its conclusion that, because Custodia’s business model was “narrowly focused on crypto-asset activities,” it presented a greater risk that was “highly likely inconsistent with safe and sound banking practices.” The 10th Circuit sided with the Fed, holding that federal law gives the Fed discretion to reject requests to open an account even if the entity making the request is otherwise eligible.

    A call for the government’s views on terrorism-related cases.

    Sources indicate that in its list of orders, the court also asked the Trump administration to weigh in on trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of the 1998 bombings at U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania, as well as victims of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The cases came to the Supreme Court in connection with the victims’ efforts to attach or receive funds from the Afghan central bank held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The victims’ petitions for review asked the justices to weigh in on how the determination of whether an entity is a “foreign state” for purposes of the federal Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, as well as the interpretation of the Terrorism Risk Insurance Act, which provides that when someone obtains a judgment against a terrorist group, they can obtain funds from the group’s seized or frozen assets.

    The United States has not recognized the Taliban as Afghanistan’s official government, and the Taliban did not file a response to the petitions. Instead, a “friend of the court” brief from the head of Afghanistan’s permanent mission to the United Nations urges the justices to deny review. He tells the court that he “supports compensation for the Taliban’s victims. But,” he continues, “it cannot come from the Afghan people, who have no liability for the Taliban’s crimes and who resisted the Taliban, at great cost, alongside the United States.”.

    Justice Elena Kagan did not participate in the decision to seek the government’s views in two of the three cases, indicating that she had recused herself from the consideration of the cases because of her prior government service – presumably as the U.S. solicitor general during the Obama administration.

    There is no deadline for the solicitor general to file his briefs.

    Comfortable in low-process, high-autonomy environments and bringing structure where it's missing.

    Able to translate technical capability into business value for both technical buyers and executive stakeholders.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that lawyer Steven Cozzi, 41, who worked for Blanchard Law, a small law firm in Largo, Florida, went missing in 2023. Dr. Tomasz Kosowski of Florida was convicted of killing Cozzi and sentenced to death Friday. (Photo courtesy of the Largo Police Department).

    A Florida judge has sentenced a prominent plastic surgeon to death for the murder of a “beloved” lawyer who went missing in 2023, saying the doctor committed the crime in a “cold, calculated and premeditated manner.”.

    Pinellas County Circuit Judge Joseph A. Bulone handed down the death sentence Friday to Dr. Tomasz Kosowski of Florida, who was convicted in September of murdering attorney Steven Cozzi, 41, whom he faced in a contentious lawsuit, Law360 reports.

    Prosecutors said Cozzi was last seen entering the restroom of his law office in Largo, Florida, in March 2023. Surveillance video allegedly captured Kosowski walking into the law office’s main entrance on the morning that Cozzi went missing, showing the surgeon carrying a backpack and a large box. About two hours later, the video demonstrates him walking out of the building with a different clothes and pulling a large cart covered with a red blanket.

    Cozzi, described as a “beloved” person, worked for Blanchard Law, a small law firm specializing in business litigation, bankruptcies and contract disputes. At the time of his disappearance, Cozzi was representing a defendant being sued by Kosowski over medical billing disputes. His body was never found.

    #101869. Treating the free exercise of religion and equal protection differently

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1898 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Treating the free exercise of religion and equal protection differently

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, two of the most enduring rights in the Constitution are the First Amendment’s protections of the free exercise of religion and the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause.
    • 3, several of the conservative justices in their questions suggested that a law’s discriminatory effect against a religion should be a basis for striking it down.
    • Industry observers note that colorado, in 2024, adopted a universal preschool program where it will provide funds for children to attend public, secular private, or faith-based preschools.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, two of the most enduring rights in the Constitution are the First Amendment’s protections of the free exercise of religion and the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause. Should the court’s approach to these rights vary? Specifically, should it be easier to prove discrimination under the free exercise clause than under equal protection?

    At the oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, on Nov. 3, several of the conservative justices in their questions suggested that a law’s discriminatory effect against a religion should be a basis for striking it down. That is in sharp contrast with a half century of law under equal protection holding that disparate impact (seemingly neutral policies that result in negative effects on a particular group) is not enough to prove discrimination. I would not be surprised to see such “free exercise exceptionalism” from the Roberts court. But it seems to me unjustified.

    Recent findings suggest that st. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy.

    Industry observers note that colorado, in 2024, adopted a universal preschool program where it will provide funds for children to attend public, secular private, or faith-based preschools. The condition for receiving funds is that the school must consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.”.

    St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colorado, which has a Catholic preschool, and two parents brought a challenge arguing that this restriction on funding violates their free exercise of religion as it requires them to accept students whose families do not adhere to the Catholic Church’s teachings, including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents. The federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit upheld the Colorado law.

    The 10th Circuit stressed that the Colorado law did not discriminate on the basis of religion. The court applied the Supreme Court’s 1990 decision in Employment Division v. Smith, which held that the free exercise clause cannot be used to challenge a neutral law of general applicability. This means that the free exercise clause is not a basis for an exception to a law unless it can be shown either that it was motivated by a desire to interfere with religion, that it discriminates against religion, or even that it just creates discretion to treat religions differently from secular actions. The 10th Circuit found that the Colorado law met the requirements for a neutral law of general applicability, as, among other things, it did not treat any one religion differently than others.

    The court of appeals also found no discrimination against religious schools in government funding. In 2017’s Trinity Lutheran v. Comer, the court declared unconstitutional a Missouri law that provided public and secular private schools funds for surfacing playgrounds that did not provide the same funds to religious schools. In 2022’s Carson v. Makin, the court applied this to invalidate a Maine law that provided funds to parents to send their children to secular private schools in areas without public schools, but not “sectarian” schools. The 10th Circuit distinguished these cases, explaining that the Colorado law did not exclude religious schools as it allowed them to receive state money on the same terms as all other preschools.

    At the oral argument on Nov. 3, there was more focus on the latter problem, perhaps because it would avoid the court needing to decide whether to overrule Employment Division v. Smith. In 2021’s Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, Justice Samuel Alito wrote an opinion concurring in the judgment, joined by Justices Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch, urging the overruling of Smith. Justice Amy Coney Barrett, joined by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, wrote a concurring opinion, expressing support for that view, but finding it unnecessary to decide the issue to resolve that case. The court likely remains divided over whether to overrule Smith and what would replace it.

    Sources indicate that in the arguments in St. Mary Catholic Parish, there were many questions from the conservative justices that suggested that they saw the Colorado law as discriminatory because of its effects on religious schools. For example, Chief Justice John Roberts asked the attorney for Colorado how this was different from the program in Carson v. Makin and mentioned that the effect of the Maine law was “pretty much the same as the effect of the law here,” as it disadvantaged religious schools. Barrett asked Colorado’s attorney why, if Colorado cannot expressly exclude religious schools from its program, it can nevertheless “impose a condition” – the nondiscrimination requirement – that it knows such “schools will be unable to agree to.”.

    In other words, these justices suggested that a discriminatory effect of Colorado’s law would be sufficient to find the law violated the free exercise of religion even though the law remarked nothing about religion and was not motivated by a desire to interfere with religion. The questions suggested that Colorado adopting the non-discrimination requirement knowing that some religious schools would not comply should be sufficient to prove discrimination under the free exercise clause.

    It has been revealed that such an approach would be dramatically different from analysis under the equal protection clause. Although I personally think such cases were incorrectly decided, the Supreme Court long has held that proof of a discriminatory effect alone is not sufficient to establish race or sex discrimination. And it has expressly held that discrimination cannot be proven by showing that government officials took an action with knowledge that it would have discriminatory consequences.

    In a recent development, washington v. Davis, decided 50 years ago, was a key case holding that a racially discriminatory effect is not sufficient to establish an equal protection violation. Applicants for the police force in Washington, D.C., were required to take a test, and statistics revealed that Black individuals failed the examination much more often than Whites. The Supreme Court, however, held that proof of a discriminatory impact is insufficient, by itself, to show the existence of a racial classification. Justice Byron White, writing for the majority, remarked that the court never had held that “a law or other official act, without regard to whether it reflects a racially discriminatory purpose, is unconstitutional solely because it has a racially disproportionate impact.” The court explained that discriminatory impact, “[s]tanding alone, . . . does not trigger the rule that racial classifications are to be subjected to the strictest scrutiny and are justifiable only by the weightiest of considerations.”.

    Sources indicate that the court has even held that discriminatory purpose cannot be proven by showing that government officials adopted a policy with knowledge that it would have a discriminatory effect. Rather, the court has made it clear that showing such a purpose requires proof that the government desired to discriminate. In 1979’s Personnel Administrator of Massachusetts v. Feeney, the court declared: “‘Discriminatory purpose,’ … implies more than intent as volition or intent as awareness of consequences. It implies that the decisionmaker . . . selected or reaffirmed a particular course of action at least in part ‘because of,’ not merely ‘in spite of,’ its adverse effects upon an identifiable group.”.

    Feeney involved a challenge to a Massachusetts law that gave preference in hiring for state jobs to veterans. At the time of the litigation, more than 98% of the veterans in the state were male, and only 1.8% were female. The result was a substantial discriminatory effect against women in hiring for state jobs. Nonetheless, based on the principles articulated above, the Supreme Court held that there was not a sex classification because the law creating a preference for veterans was facially sex neutral and there was not proof that the state’s purpose in adopting the law was to disadvantage women. The fact that the legislature knew there would be an discriminatory effect against women was thus irrelevant.

    Recent findings suggest that there is no way to reconcile this equal protection jurisprudence with the approach several conservative justices suggested in St. Mary Catholic Parish. The question then becomes whether there is any reason to treat discrimination under the free exercise clause differently from under the equal protection clause.

    Several justices suggested in their questions at oral argument that Sherbet v. Verner, a 1963 case, justifies concluding that discriminatory impact is alone sufficient for a free exercise violation. That case involved a state having denied unemployment benefits to a woman, a member of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, who quit her job rather than work on her Saturday Sabbath. The court concluded that the denial of benefits imposed a substantial burden on religion; the woman had to choose between an income and her faith. The court thus remarked that the issue was “whether some compelling state interest enforced in the eligibility provisions of the . . . statute justifies the substantial infringement of appellant’s First Amendment right.” The court found no such compelling interest and ruled that the denial of benefits constituted a violation of the free exercise clause.

    Sherbert found a violation of the free exercise of religion based on the impact on her religion despite the law at problem being facially neutral. As a precedent for striking down the Colorado law, however, that is unpersuasive. Sherbert was decided a decade before the Supreme Court held that proof of discriminatory impact was not sufficient for an equal protection violation. And although the court has not overruled Sherbert, it has never explained how it can be reconciled with Employment Division v. Smith. But most importantly, invoking Sherbert begs the crucial question: Should a different standard be used for discrimination under the free exercise clause compared to the equal protection clause?

    In a recent development, conceptually, I cannot understand any reason why discrimination on the basis of religion should be treated dissimilarly from discrimination based on race or sex. Why should two such critical rights be treated differently? Indeed, it is just a doctrinal accident that religious discrimination is litigated under the free exercise clause (or the establishment clause) rather than the equal protection clause.

    Sources indicate that applying equal protection principles, the Colorado law does not discriminate against religion in its terms or in its purpose. Many commentators, including me, have argued that – despite court precedent – discriminatory impact should be enough for a claim under equal protection. But there has been no suggestion from the court that it is moving in that direction.

    Finally, it is important to stress that even if the law is deemed discriminatory, that does not mean that it is automatically unconstitutional. It means that strict scrutiny should be applied, in which the government action can be upheld if there is a compelling purpose for it. I was disappointed that the conservative justices did not focus on the government’s compelling interest in preventing children from being discriminated against on account of their gender identity or for having LGBTQ parents. Without explicitly saying so, the justices appear poised to carve out a special place for the free exercise clause over that of equal protection.

    In a recent development, erwin Chemerinsky is the Dean and Jesse H. Choper Distinguished Professor of Law, University of California, Berkeley School of Law.

    In a recent development, recommended Citation: Erwin Chemerinsky, Treating the free exercise of religion and equal protection differently , SCOTUSblog (Nov. 17, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/treating-the-free-exercise-of-religion-and-equal-protection-differently/.

    Tech Report: Fourth Circuit rejects Virginia ICE mask ban but OKs local cooperation

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • While Virginia can now limit ICE's immigration enforcement actions, it can't require officers to identify themselves.
    • It has been revealed that RICHMOND, Va.
    • Industry observers note that citing the principle of dual sovereignty, the three-judge panel said Virginia could restrict localities’ ability to work with U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    While Virginia can now limit ICE's immigration enforcement actions, it can't require officers to identify themselves.

    It has been revealed that RICHMOND, Va. (CN) â A Fourth Circuit panel issued a mixed bag ruling Monday for Virginia Democrats who sought to rein in misconduct from federal immigration officials.

    Industry observers note that citing the principle of dual sovereignty, the three-judge panel said Virginia could restrict localities’ ability to work with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials, but can’t require ICE agents to identify themselves by unmasking.

    In a recent development, “We question neither the sincerity nor the reasonableness of the commonwealth’s objections to masked and otherwise-unidentified law enforcement activities, and we emphasize that states may limit or forbid such conduct by their own state and local officers,” noted U.S. Circuit Judge Toby Heytens, a Joe Biden appointee who authored the opinion. “But just as Congress may not ‘glitch orders directly to the states,’ states may not issue orders directly to the federal government.”.

    Sources indicate that U.S. District Judge Robert Payne, a George H.W. Bush appointee, had blocked the laws over the summer after the Democrat-led Virginia General Assembly passed the bills in spring.

    Heytens said Payne correctly concluded that the law prohibiting ICE officials from wearing masks violates the intergovernmental immunity doctrine. But Heytens disagreed on Payne’s conclusion that a law restricting 287(g) cooperation agreements violates the contracts clause and the intergovernmental immunity doctrine.

    âTodayâs decision upholding Virginiaâs new law governing 287(g) agreements is a significant victory for Virginia and reaffirms the commonwealthâs authority to determine whether and under what conditions state and local resources may be used to assist federal immigration enforcement efforts," Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones remarked in a statement.

    It has been revealed that the conditions the law imposes on localities to continue working with ICE include ICE refraining from enforcement actions at schools, churches, and polling places and refraining from using surveillance technology. The law also bars the localities from assisting in immigration operations unless presented with a valid judicial warrant, subpoena or detainer.

    “The intergovernmental immunity doctrine does not apply because the 287(g) law neither directly regulates the federal government nor prevents private parties from contracting with it,” Heytens said. “Its arguments get basic federalism principles backward.”.

    Industry observers note that heytens pointed to the Supreme Court’s 1992 ruling in *New York v. United States,*where the majority ruled that the federal government could not commandeer the state government to participate in a federal regulatory program. He also cited other Supreme Court cases that prohibit the federal government from forcing state or local officials to enforce federal law.

    “The federal government could not order the commonwealth’s own agents â be they state or local officials â to enforce federal law, much less do so at their own expense,” Heytens wrote. “Just as the commonwealth was allowed to make one choice in the past, it is allowed to make a different choice in the future. Indeed, that is the essence of democratic self-government.”.

    Heytens noted that, unlike in the cases the federal government cites where a state prevents private parties from contracting with the federal government, the Virginia law concerns local governments. Heytens also said the law doesn’t violate the contract clause because it doesn’t affect existing contracts; instead, it restricts future ones.

    “The federal government cannot conscript our local officers into its mass deportation machine, and the General Assembly has every right to set the terms on which our own agencies cooperate,” State Senator Saddam Azlan Salim, a Democrat, mentioned in a statement. “Our communities are safer for it, because public safety depends on trust, and trust disappears when a call for help can turn into a deportation.”.

    According to recent reports, the masking law required ICE officials to wear identifiable items on their clothing and prohibits facial coverings. Heytens agreed with Payne that the state lacks the authority to tell immigration officials how to do their jobs.

    According to recent reports, U.S. Circuit Judge Robert King dissented from the majority on the facial covering law. King mentioned the injunction erroneously restricts Virginia’s traditional police powers.

    “As those of us seasoned enough to receive Social Security know, the good guys in the Western movies of our youth â played by the likes of Roy Rogers, Gene Autry, Tom Mix and John Wayne â were always recognizable,” the 83-year-old Bill Clinton appointee remarked. “Again, they were the heroes, the good guys.Â  Only the bad guys â the bank robbers and the stagecoach bandits â wore masks.”.

    Sources indicate that the federal government did not respond to a request for comment. U.S. Circuit Judge DeAndrea Gist Benjamin, a fellow Biden appointee, concurred with Heytens.

    The marbled murrelet nests in mossy cups on the tall branches of old-growth trees.

    In a recent development, PORTLAND, Ore. (CN) â On the coast of Oregon, the marbled murrelet has long been seen diving into marine waters to forage for fish. But its population has declined, and a conservation group is targeting the Trump administration for allowing its forest habitat to be disrupted.

    The Center for Biological Diversity sued the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the U.S. Bureau of Land Management on Monday, accusing the agencies of failing to protect the birds from logging in western Oregon.

    âThe Bureau of Land Managementâs logging practices are undermining marbled murreletsâ already slim chance of recovery in Oregon,â Lia Comerford, a senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity, noted in a statement.

    According to recent reports, the Bureau of Land Management adopted new intends for almost 2.5 million acres in western Oregon in 2016. The plans were designed to increase logging and maintain protections for murrelets and other species that depend on mature and old-growth forests.

    According to recent reports, as part of those plans, the agency consulted with the Fish and Wildlife Service to prepare a 200-page biological assessment on the plans’ effect on marbled murrelets and their habitat. The service concluded the Bureau of Land Managementâs plans were consistent with the Murrelet Recovery Plan.

    It has been revealed that but two years later, the bureau modified its interpretation of those protections. The group states the bureauâs fresh interpretation differs significantly from the version the service consulted on and fundamentally undermines the serviceâs analysis of how the aims will affect murrelets and their habitat.

    Specifically, the group says the interpretations made it so key protections are triggered far less frequently. The Fish and Wildlife Service then approved those reduced protections, in what the group called a âhighly cursory, incomplete, and arbitrary and capricious manner,â paving the way for logging in murrelet habitat.

    Neither agency made the changes publicly available, the group claims.

    âUnder the first Trump administration, officials at the agency went back on a promise to protect these precious seabirdsâ habitat,â Comerford said. âWeâre not going to let them get away with it.â.

    The marbled murrelet has been listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act since 1992.

    Recent findings suggest that the seabirds nest high in large trees in old-growth forests and fly up to 55 miles inland during breeding season from late spring to fall. Murrelets nest in small, mossy cups on large branches high off the ground, typically only in large, old trees.

    According to recent reports, murrelets generally lay only one egg per year, leading to the species’ naturally low reproductive rate. Mated murrelets take shifts flying from the nest to the ocean to forage for fish while incubating the single egg. Marbled murrelets have high âsite fidelity,â meaning they often return to the same trees year to year.

    Logging can displace breeding murrelets and lower nest success by removing trees with nesting platforms. Forest clearing can also increase predation. Crows, jays and ravens prey upon marbled murrelet nests and proliferate near forest edges.

    According to the group, scientists have recommended a 300- to 600-foot buffer around occupied murrelet habitat for decades.

    The Significant Weekly Elk Project, which the bureau approved in 2021, includes logging in and around nesting habitat. The Center for Biological Diversity claims the bureau is ignoring murrelet protections and has already sold numerous timber sales under the project.

    The group is asking a federal judge to find both agencies violated the Endangered Species Act and block the Bureau of Land Management from authorizing or implementing any logging activities.

    âThe Bureau of Land Management has abandoned the protections it agreed to 10 years ago and is trying to maximize logging at the expense of these very imperiled birds,â stated Comerford. âSadly, the Fish and Wildlife Service is just sitting on its hands, letting marbled murrelets spiral further toward extinction.â.

    The groupâs lawsuit follows the Trump administrationâs announcement of its intent to patch resource management looks for western Oregon to increase logging.

    The Bureau of Land Management declined to comment on pending litigation, but said it will continue to work closely with its partners to fulfill its public land and conservation responsibilities.

    #101864. Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1587 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scotusblog ↗ Open Full Page

    Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1587 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scotusblog

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing.
    • In a recent development, until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a).
    • Recent findings suggest that under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal proceedings end is discretionary, case-by-case parole, granted only for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, on Oct. 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing. This question now sits at the court in two pieces: a statutory question the justices have agreed to answer, and a constitutional one still waiting for the right case. Together, the answers will decide whether people who have lived here for years, even decades, can ask a judge to release them while they fight deportation.

    In a recent development, until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a). According to this provision, ICE may release a detainee on bond subject to an immigration judge’s review (unless Section 1226(c)’s criminal- and terrorism-related provisions apply). In July 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement began requiring – for the first time – that anyone who had entered the United States without inspection, whether last year or decades ago, be detained instead under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) for the length of removal proceedings. Unlike Section 1226(a), this provision holds that immigration judges have no power to grant such detainees bond. Two months later, the Board of Immigration Appeals agreed with ICE in Matter of Yajure Hurtado.

    Recent findings suggest that under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal proceedings end is discretionary, case-by-case parole, granted only for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit. Partly due to this policy, ICE’s overall detained population, which also includes people held on other grounds, hit a reported record of roughly 73,000 in mid-January 2026.

    Section 1225(a)(1) deems any noncitizen “present in the United States who has not been admitted [to the country]” to be an “applicant for admission.” The detention command then provides: “in the case of an alien who is an applicant for admission, if the examining immigration officer determines that an alien seeking admission is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, the alien shall be detained.” The courts of appeals agree that long-term residents who entered the U.S. unlawfully are deemed “applicant[s] for admission.” The dispute is whether that deemed status also means they are “seeking admission,” and would thus fall within Section 1225 and be detainable without bond.

    Recent findings suggest that eleven of the 12 federal circuit courts (all but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit) have now answered. Nine hold that Section 1226, not Section 1225(b)(2)(A), governs people arrested in the interior: the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 6th, 7th, 9th, 10th and 11th Circuits. Two read Section 1225(b)(2)(A) as the government does: the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 5th Circuit and the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 8th Circuit.

    According to recent reports, for the majority of circuits, “seeking admission” is an ordinary phrase Congress left undefined, and as the 1st Circuit put it, “means seeking lawful entry.” A person who crossed the border years ago is not seeking entry; he already entered. The deeming clause in Section 1225(a)(1) may make a long-term resident an applicant for admission, Judge Joshua Kolar wrote for the 7th Circuit, but it does not “conjure a fictional intent to seek admission.” Structure points the same way: in the Laken Riley Act of January 2025, Congress expanded Section 1226(c)’s mandatory detention categories to reach certain unlawful entrants accused or convicted of specified offenses, a needless step if Section 1225 had always reached them. The majority of circuits add that five administrations over three decades read the statute their way, and that Congress would not silently have required detaining some two million people.

    It has been revealed that for the 5th and 8th Circuits, however, ordinary meaning cuts differently. To apply for something is to seek it, Judge Edith Jones wrote for the 5th Circuit; for example, a college applicant does not stop seeking admission once the application is filed. Several dissenters elsewhere go further and rest on the deeming clause itself, arguing that a legal fiction carries the attributes of the thing it deems. As 11th Circuit Judge Barbara Lagoa wrote in dissent, in a line later adopted by a 1st Circuit dissenter: “If a person whom Congress has deemed an applicant for admission is not seeking admission, it is hard to know what Congress thought it was deeming him to be.”.

    According to recent reports, as for the government’s long contrary practice: “Years of consistent practice,” Jones wrote, “cannot vindicate an interpretation that is inconsistent with a statute’s plain text.” Government-side judges answer the Laken Riley point, too: Section 1226(c) also reaches admitted noncitizens and bars parole, and in January 2025 DHS still treated unlawful entrants as bond-eligible. Both sides now also cite the justices’ own June decision in Mullin v. Al Otro Lado, which read “arrives in the United States” to mean crossing the border, stated fears of encouraging illegal entry “cannot defeat the best reading of the text,” and called the rule that every word must do work “not an iron rule.”.

    Sources indicate that the Supreme Court will soon have its say. On Oct. 1, the justices agreed to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, the government’s challenge to a unanimous 2nd Circuit panel ruling for a Brazilian man who has lived here more than 20 years, was detained in 2025 under Section 1225(b)(2)(A), and which that circuit court found to be inapplicable. No argument date is set yet; proposed merits briefing runs into February, pointing to argument in late winter or spring and a decision by term’s end.

    But a related constitutional question is also pending at the court. This is whether, even if under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) detainees do not have a statutory right to a bond hearing, they have a right to one under the due process clause. On Oct. 23, the full U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit held in the case of Sosnava Rodriguez v. Vergara that noncitizens subject to the government’s mandatory detention policy have no such right.

    Judge Cory Wilson wrote for the majority: “Because Petitioners have never been admitted to the United States, due process does not entitle them to additional proceedings beyond what Congress has provided before they may be detained pending removal.” Seven judges dissented. Judge Leslie Southwick countered that the court “has constructed an impenetrable wall between the Constitution and these long-term residents,” who by the record had each lived here for more than a decade.

    For now, in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi, noncitizens who entered without inspection thus have no ordinary path to a bond hearing; discretionary parole and a few claims the majority reserved remain, but those are narrow exits. The 8th Circuit’s ruling closes the statutory route across its seven states as well.

    In a recent development, the 3rd and 6th Circuits, on the other hand, have held that detaining long-present noncitizens under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) without a bond hearing does indeed violate due process. In these circuits, which cover Delaware, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and the U.S. Virgin Islands (the 3rd Circuit), and Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and Tennessee (the 6th Circuit), long-term residents can point to circuit precedent recognizing a due process right to a bond hearing. One’s geographical location thus makes all the difference.

    Sources indicate that if the court affirms in Rhoney, subject to specific exceptions, noncitizens who entered without inspection and are later arrested in the interior could again ask for bond everywhere, as they could before July 2025. A hearing does not guarantee release, and the burden is generally on the detainee, but the right to ask for bond would be the same in every circuit. If the court reverses in Rhoney, mandatory detention becomes the statutory rule everywhere, yet geography, as noted, would still matter: the 3rd and 6th Circuits have held that a constitutional right to due process requires bond hearings for long-resident detainees like those before them, and the 5th has held it does not.

    That is where the case of Putra v. Lopez-Campos comes in. The government’s petition from its loss in the 6th Circuit in that case raises both the statutory and constitutional questions, and the solicitor general urged the justices to take it for that reason. The court only agreed to hear Rhoney, which raises the statutory question, and thus appears to be holding Putra until Rhoney is decided. If the government wins in Rhoney, the split between the 3rd and 6th Circuits, which found a due process right to a bond hearing, and the 5th, which did not, would matter far more, and the justices would likely have to take up Putra to settle the due process issue. But if the detainees win in Rhoney, that constitutional question may never need an answer.

    According to recent reports, rhoney should be decided before the term ends next summer. Based on this decision, we will see if the constitutional dispute follows. In the meantime, tens of thousands of people remain detained.

    Kemal Hepsen is the managing attorney of Hepsen Law Firm, a federal litigation firm that represents noncitizens nationwide in habeas corpus, mandamus, and Administrative Procedure Act cases.

    Tech Report: 11th Circuit tosses ex-Georgia Tech professor’s lawsuit against university auditors

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (717 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Courthousenews

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The 11th Circuit panel found that the former Georgia Tech professor's racketeering charges stemmed from an independent investigation by state authorities, not a university audit.
    • (CN) â An 11th Circuit panel rejected a former Georgia Tech professorâs suit against two university auditors he blamed for his arrest in a racketeering case.
    • Circuit Judge William Pryor wrote in a unanimous opinion issued Monday that Joy Laskar failed to establish that the auditors, Phillip Hurd and Patrick Jenkins, conducted the investigation that led to his prosecution.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The 11th Circuit panel found that the former Georgia Tech professor's racketeering charges stemmed from an independent investigation by state authorities, not a university audit.

    (CN) â An 11th Circuit panel rejected a former Georgia Tech professorâs suit against two university auditors he blamed for his arrest in a racketeering case.

    Chief U.S. Circuit Judge William Pryor wrote in a unanimous opinion issued Monday that Joy Laskar failed to establish that the auditors, Phillip Hurd and Patrick Jenkins, conducted the investigation that led to his prosecution. Laskarâs charges stemmed from an independent investigation conducted by state authorities â not the university officials’ internal audit or their report of suspected misconduct, the panel found.

    Industry observers note that âBefore obtaining an arrest warrant, Agent Vorrasi and McLaughlin conducted an independent investigation,â the George W. Bush appointee wrote in the opinion. âThey reviewed the same documents reviewed during the audit. They spent four months analyzing thousands of documents, deposing Sayana employees and consulting other university officials.â.

    In a recent development, laskar was director of the Georgia Electronic Design Center, a research center where tech companies collaborate with researchers after paying membership dues. He was also co-founder and president of Sayana, a manufacturer that designed and developed high-frequency microchips.

    According to recent reports, in 2009, Georgia Tech began investigating a $600,000 shortfall at the center, according to court filings. Hurd and Jenkins learned during their audit that Sayana had billed the design center more than $1 million for the manufacture of prototype microchips which were later sent to a South Korean institute, which paid for the prototypes and research.

    Laskar failed to disclose in conflict-of-interest reports filed with the university between 2007 and 2010 that he had a 42.5% stake in Sayana, according to the auditors. Sayana also did not pay membership fees to use the centerâs resources.

    The auditors reported the suspected malfeasance to the university, which in turn sent the report to the Georgia Department of Law.

    Laskar was charged in 2010 with two counts of racketeering, but a Superior Court judge dismissed the case four years later after finding the statute of limitations barred the charges.

    Laskar filed a civil rights action against the auditors in 2018 in the Northern District of Georgia, claiming the government employees intentionally provided false and misleading information to law enforcement.

    Industry observers note that U.S. District Judge William M. Ray, a Donald Trump appointee, initially dismissed the case because Laskar did not receive a âfavorable terminationâ in criminal court, or a finding of innocence, which could maintain a malicious prosecution suit. The decision was reversed on appeal, but Ray dismissed it again last year after finding Laskar failed to support his claims that the auditors operated as law enforcement officers.

    The 11th Circuit panel appeared skeptical of Laskarâs arguments during a hearing this month.

    U.S. Circuit Judge Embry Kidd, a Joe Biden appointee, suggested the auditorsâ recommendation was no different from any other tip to law enforcement.

    Recent findings suggest that âSometimes investigations rely heavily on information provided by others,â he mentioned. âThat does not mean that the decision by the investigator wasnât independent of the people providing the information.â.

    Pryor mentioned it did not matter if the auditors provided advice and information to state authorities. The investigators specifically stated that their warrant application was based on their independent investigation and their own assessment of the evidence.

    Industry observers note that pryor filed a separate concurring opinion Monday addressing the U.S. Supreme Courtâs decision in Thompson v. Clark, which determined a plaintiff only needs to show that a prosecution ended without a conviction to establish the “favorable termination” element for a malicious prosecution case.

    Pryor defended the use of the common-law tort of malicious prosecution as the appropriate analogy for constitutional claims involving seizures pursuant to legal process, such as arrests based on warrants.

    He distinguished those claims from challenges to warrantless arrests, explaining that the two types of seizures involve different legal considerations.

    U.S. Circuit Judge Barbara Lagoa, a Trump appointee, rounded out the panel.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The justices of the Supreme Court aren’t scheduled to meet for a private conference – and vote on new petitions for review – for two-and-a-half weeks.
    • The federal government and President Donald Trump are at the center of three of the biggest petitions for review up for consideration on Dec.
    • Talbott, the justices will decide whether to review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that bars the Trump administration from expelling several transgender servicemembers from the military.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The justices of the Supreme Court aren’t scheduled to meet for a private conference – and vote on new petitions for review – for two-and-a-half weeks. But when they do, on Friday, Dec. 4, they will have a number of high-profile cases to consider – which could, in turn, lead to a busy spring.

    The federal government and President Donald Trump are at the center of three of the biggest petitions for review up for consideration on Dec. 4.

    In United States v. Talbott, the justices will decide whether to review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that bars the Trump administration from expelling several transgender servicemembers from the military.

    In a recent development, in the government’s petition for review, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer called the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit “gravely erroneous” and argued that its “reasoning cannot be squared with this Court’s precedents or deference to the military.”.

    It has been revealed that the challengers urged the court to stay out of the dispute, calling the D.C. Circuit’s decision “narrow” and temporary. And in any event, they added, the ruling is correct, because the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers was motivated by hostility to transgender people rather than “military judgments.”.

    In a recent development, in another case to be considered, Trump and the federal government have each filed petitions for review in connection with Trump’s challenge to the $83.3 million verdict entered against him in a lawsuit brought by E. Jean Carroll, who had alleged that in 1996 Trump had sexually abused her in a dressing room at a Fresh York department store and that Trump in 2019 had defamed her by calling her a liar.

    In a recent development, trump’s petition for review points to the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Trump v. United States, in which it held that presidents generally have broad immunity for their acts while in office. Trump’s private attorney, Robert Giuffra, wrote that “[t]he threat of even a single damages judgment based on official acts will render all Presidents ‘unable to boldly and fearlessly carry out [their] duties for fear that [they] may be next.’”.

    The federal government’s petition for review asks the Supreme Court to also decide whether the federal government, rather than Trump, should be the defendant in Carroll’s case because Trump made the statements at the center of the dispute as part of his role as president.

    And in United States v. Jackson and United States v. Office of the New York State Attorney General, the justices will decide whether to weigh in on the legality of Trump’s appointments of acting U.S. attorneys in Nevada and New York.

    Sources indicate that under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, the federal law that governs how the executive branch can temporarily staff vacant positions that require presidential appointment and confirmation by the Senate, interim officers can serve for 120 days. Under that law, then-Attorney General Pamela Bondi appointed Sigal Chattah as the interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Nevada, effective April 1, 2025, after Jason Frierson, who was nominated by then-President Joe Biden, stepped down.

    With only a few days remaining before her interim appointment was set to expire, Chattah resigned, and Bondi designated her as the first assistant U.S. attorney. In that post, Bondi said, Chattah would have the power under the FVRA “to serve as Acting United States Attorney upon a vacancy in that office.” Bondi also gave Chattah the powers of a U.S. attorney for legal proceedings in Nevada.

    According to recent reports, bondi followed a similar path for John Sarcone in the Northern District of Upcoming York, naming him first as the interim U.S. Attorney and then, when his interim term expired, naming him as the first assistant U.S. attorney and a “special attorney,” effectively designating him as the “Acting U.S. Attorney.”.

    In a recent development, when challenges to the legitimacy of Chattah’s and Sarcone’s appointments followed, lower courts agreed that neither had been validly appointed. Sauer then came to the Supreme Court, where he told the justices that Chattah’s appointment was not only lawful, but “a critical tool that the Executive Branch has used without meaningful objection for 25 years.” He urged the court to take up that case, and to hold the New York case until the Nevada case is resolved.

    In addition to those disputes, the justices will consider three other noteworthy petitions for review on Dec. 4:.

    It has been revealed that one thing to keep in mind: although the justices are slated to vote on these cases for the first time on Dec. 4, they may not act on any of them right away. In particular, for several years, the court has had a general practice of not granting a petition for review until the justices have considered it at two conferences. After the Dec. 4 conference, the justices will meet again on Dec. 11.

    Recent findings suggest that finally, yet another high-profile petition for review is likely to be before the justices soon: Trump v. Clinton, in which Trump is seeking to revive his lawsuit against Hillary Clinton (and several others, including the Democratic National Committee) alleging “a coordinated scheme … to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion.” Clinton originally waived her right to file a response to Trump’s petition, but the court called for a response, which she filed on Nov. 13. In her response, Clinton contends that “President Donald Trump and his attorneys” “attempt to frame a routine opinion disposing of a frivolous lawsuit as a threat to ‘the Presidency.’”.

    Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

    Trump declared a national emergency in a 2025 executive order with respect to any ICC effort to investigate, arrest, detain or prosecute “any United States person” unless the U.S. formally consents or becomes a state party to the Rome Statute, which established the ICC in 2002 to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity.

    Recent findings suggest that judges Kimberly Prost, Solomy Bossa and Reine Alapini-Gansou of the ICC turned to the U.S. courts asking to be removed from the sanctions list, unblock their frozen property and bar Trump from enforcing measures against them. But U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman dismissed all but one of their claims and denied a preliminary injunction, finding “deference here is owed not only to the president but also to Congress.”.

    “In short, whatever the courtâs own assessment of the circumstances may be, plaintiffsâ allegations do not permit the court to hold that the president acted ultra vires when he declared a national emergency to address what he determined to be an ‘unusual and extraordinary threat, which has its source in whole or substantial part outside the United States,’ to the national security, foreign policy, or economy of the United States,” Furman wrote in a 37-page order.

    Each judge was sanctioned over a different decision. Prost, of Canada, and Bossa, of the Republic of Uganda, joined a 2020 appeals ruling that allowed the ICC prosecutor to investigate suspected war crimes and crimes against humanity in Afghanistan. Alapini-Gansou, of the Republic of Benin, sat on the panel that approved arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant.

    Recent findings suggest that the trio of judges sued under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, U.S. Constitution and Administrative Procedure Act. Furman, a Barack Obama appointee, dismissed the due process and takings clause claims, but preserved the plaintiffs’ APA claim accusing the federal government of arbitrary and capricious sanctions designations. That count is premature, the judge mentioned, since it must be decided on the full administrative record that was before Secretary of State Marco Rubio when he made the decision.

    Furman noted there are three other cases in Manhattan federal court involving challenges to Trump’s executive order, but unlike the others, the trio of judges don’t bring First Amendment claims and are challenging the order in its entirety.

    Industry observers note that those other, earlier lawsuits filed by U.S. human rights advocates resulted in rulings barring the administration from enforcing the order against Americans providing speech-based services to the ICC.

    Recent findings suggest that trump signed Executive Order 14203 on Feb. 6, 2025, after the ICC pursued investigations involving U.S. personnel in Afghanistan and Israeli leaders over the war in Gaza.

    After first sanctioning ICC prosecutor Karim Khan, the White House expanded its list to include the international courtâs two deputy prosecutors, eight judges, U.N. Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese and three Palestinian human rights organizations: Al-Haq, Al Mezan Center for Human Rights and the Palestinian Center for Human Rights.

    Recent findings suggest that the sanctions formally freeze U.S.-based assets and bar Americans from providing funds or services. The judges say their effects ripple across global banks, payment systems and technology companies that rely heavily on the U.S. financial system.

    âThe sanctions regime punishes Judges Prost, Bossa and Alapini-Gansou for having done nothing more than â when called upon to adjudicate matters before them â faithfully discharge their judicial offices by rendering decisions with which the administration disagrees,â the judges say in their lawsuit.

    In addition to arguing that the sanctions strike at the independence of international courts by punishing judges for carrying out their duties, the judges say Trump’s order disrupts ICC investigations that Republican and Democratic administrations alike have backed over the years, including cases involving Sudan, Libya, Uganda, Mali, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Ukraine.

This role is for someone who'd rather design for one very specific, very opinionated person: the developer at 2am trying to figure out why their voice agent just failed a call. You'll design the tools developers use to test, evaluate and debug AI agents — a category that's still being invented, with no established patterns to copy. If dense data, real-time systems and reading a stack trace sound more fun than intimidating, keep reading.

    You'll thrive as a Senior Product Designer if you:.

    are obsessed with making the best product for our customers.

    are known as the go-to person for tackling tough problems.

    work hard and can build and ship fast.

    are focused on polish, detail and quality.

    are a fast learner, frequently picking up fresh tips, tricks, and skills.

    The best way to impress us is with thoughtful ways you'd implement LiveKit, and potentially tinkering with it 😊.

    Own the design of how developers test, evaluate and observe their agents — simulations, evals, logs and agent insights.

    Turn complex, real-time data into interfaces that are easy to scan, understand and act on.

    Design new interaction patterns for AI-native workflows, where agents generate the first draft and humans adjust it.

    Prototype in code and work hand-in-hand with engineers to ship polished work.

    Contribute patterns to our design system for dense, debugging-oriented surfaces.

    You've shipped design work for developer tools, observability or data-heavy products.

    You have strong data-visualization instincts and know when a chart beats a table (and when it doesn't).

    You're comfortable in code — reading PRs, tweaking Tailwind, building prototypes.

    You earn the trust of deeply technical owners and engineers.

    Experience designing for AI or agent tooling.

    AI tools are already a core part of how you design.

    An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world.

    Contribute to open source alongside world-class engineers.

    Competitive salary and equity package.

    Health, dental, and vision benefits.

    Quebec politicians will have to pledge an oath to King Charles III or risk legal battles over their laws.

    MONTREAL (CN) â The Superior Court of Quebec ruled Monday that a 2022 law allowing members of the province’s National Assembly to pledge allegiance only to Quebecers, and not to the British king, is unconstitutional.

    The decision sparked waves of protests from Quebec politicians, putting the upcoming legislative session in limbo.

    According to recent reports, superior Court Justice Ian Demers found the provincial government overstepped its powers by abolishing the king’s oath without the approval of Ottawa and the other provinces. He ruled in favor of Lawrence David, a University of Ottawa law professor who challenged the legislation in August.

    According to recent reports, the judge agreed with David that suspending the law is necessary to avoid chaos in the National Assembly. The professor and founder of the Public Interest Litigation Institute argued that laws adopted by members of the National Assembly who had not pledged their allegiance to King Charles III would be invalid and that the law violated Quebecers’ right to proper representation.

    David also claimed the oath could be abolished only with the unanimous consent of the provinces and the federal Parliament, because the change encroached on the role of the lieutenant governor. Canada is a constitutional monarchy, and lieutenant governors represent the Crown.

    The Legislature adopted Bill 4 in December 2022, after the three Parti QuÃ©bÃ©cois members elected that year refused to swear the oath required by the Constitution Act of 1867, and were barred from taking their seats in the National Assembly.

    It has been revealed that quebec politicians appear to agree with the law. None of the 127 members of the National Assembly elected in October has sworn allegiance to the king. The court nonetheless found the law unconstitutional.

    Industry observers note that “The Constitution is not an Ã  la carte menu in which a subject complies with what suits them,” Demers wrote in his ruling. “Any other proposal would lead to constitutional disorder, or even chaos.”.

    “If the stay were not ordered, all laws passed by the National Assembly would be unconstitutional and would have to be reenacted,” he added, predicting the process would only “paralyze” the government and harm Quebecers.

    Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, Parti Quebecois leader â and former lawyer â denounced the decision.

    “The government of Quebec strongly condemns a ruling that clearly goes against the democratic will of Quebecers, who have expressed their desire to put an end to the disloyal act of swearing an oath to the British monarch and to the straitjacket of the monarchy in general,” the premier stated in a statement released on social media in French.

    In a press conference in Montreal on Monday, St-Pierre Plamondon called the ruling a “disgrace” and said he “cannot take an oath to the king of England.” He vowed to take all necessary measures to oppose the judgment.

    The premier noted Quebec never signed the 1982 Canadian Constitution, and that the Constitutional Act of 1867 was imposed on the French-Canadian people after the British conquest of the French territory. He insists Quebecers should be allowed to follow the democratic process rather than be forced to follow rules imposed on them.

    It has been revealed that the legislative assembly set for Dec. 1 is now up in the air. Lawmakers must decide between swearing allegiance to the king and risking court challenges to every decision they make.

    All the opposition parties also criticized the ruling and welcomed the government’s appeal, deploring that the decision could push back further the start of the National Assembly.

    The Parti Quebecois has long been fighting the presence of the monarchy in Quebec. St-Pierre Plamondon promised earlier this year to abolish the Office of the Lieutenant Governor of Quebec, or at least divert its resources to fight problems such as the homelessness crisis.

    Courthouse News reporter Tatiana Mulowayi-Pelletier is based in Montreal, Canada.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • A woman arrested two years ago for panhandling in a northwestern New Mexico city wants a federal court to find a panhandling ordinance unconstitutional.
    • Recent findings suggest that ALBUQUERQUE, N.M.
    • Two years after her arrest, she’s suing the northwestern Newly introduced Mexico city of Farmington over its sweeping panhandling ban, arguing that holding a cardboard sign requesting money is constitutionally protected speech.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    A woman arrested two years ago for panhandling in a northwestern New Mexico city wants a federal court to find a panhandling ordinance unconstitutional.

    Recent findings suggest that ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. â Rebecca Serrano-Himmel indicates she was sitting in a strip mall parking lot with a sign requesting money in March 2024 when police cited and trespassed her from the property. Four months later, she was arrested when displaying a similar sign at an intersection.

    Two years after her arrest, she’s suing the northwestern Newly introduced Mexico city of Farmington over its sweeping panhandling ban, arguing that holding a cardboard sign requesting money is constitutionally protected speech.

    It has been revealed that in her suit filed Monday in Upcoming Mexico federal court, Serrano-Himmel seeks damages against the city and its police officers for unreasonable seizure and deprivation of free speech, as well as a declaration that the ordinance violates the First and Fourteenth Amendments of the U.S. Constitution.

    Industry observers note that farmington Mayor Nate Duckett, a defendant in the suit, signed the panhandling ordinance in February 2023. It prohibits the solicitation of money or goods on public and private property.

    “Since the passing of the ordinance and still after the receipt of the letter alerting the mayor and the city attorney about the unconstitutionality of the ordinance, Duckett continued to enforce the panhandling ordinance in a manner that deprived multiple people of their first amendment right to free speech,” Serrano-Himmel writes in the complaint.

    According to Serrano-Himmel, holding a sign requesting money in a public space is protected speech under the U.S. Constitution and the state constitution.

    This ordinance allowed city police officers to cease her speech and retaliate against her as a result of her exercising her free speech, she says.

    In her first run-in with city police in March 2024, Serrano-Himmel says Officer Aaron Favaloro seized her identification to check for outstanding warrants and issued a citation for panhandling and a trespass notice, despite having no ownership or control over the property.

    Serrano-Himmel asserted throughout the interaction that she was engaging in lawful behavior. In response, Favaloro threatened to arrest her. She was found not guilty of panhandling in July 2024.

    Two weeks later, city police officer Marcus Martinez approached Serrano-Himmel after spotting her walking in a parking lot with a sign stating she was homeless and requesting assistance.

    It has been revealed that serrano-Himmel says Martinez told her she was panhandling, which was not allowed in city limits. She continued to state that she was acting lawfully. Martinez then arrested her for panhandling and criminal trespass and seized her sign.

    The officers’ actions violate Serrano-Himmel’s First Amendment right, which protects her speech, and Fourth Amendment right, which protects her against unreasonable seizures, Serrano-Himmel writes in the complaint. Both officers are named as defendants in the suit, alongside Duckett and the city of Farmington.

    According to recent reports, serrano-Himmel’s attorney, Joseph P. Kennedy of The Kennedy Law Firm, has challenged the ordinance before, according to Serrano-Himmel.

    Kennedy gave notice to Farmington that non-party Jerry Sullivan was suing the city in August 2023 after Sullivan had been detained for panhandling.

    Sherald Daniels, also represented by Kennedy, sued over the ordinance in another federal lawsuit earlier this year after receiving a citation for playing music in a public space.

    “The city has enforced the ordinance repeatedly in a manner that has damaged and deprived the free-speech rights of residents and visitors,” Serrano-Himmel writes.

    Farmington city attorneys declined to provide comment. Kennedy did not respond to a request for comment before publication.
